hero.headline: North Palm Beach hosts Fourth of July fireworks and pool party at country club
hero.teaser: North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse will host a full day of free community activities on July 4, including a pool party, live music, lawn games and fireworks at 9 p.m.
hero.body:
North Palm Beach residents and visitors will celebrate Independence Day with a full day of family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4. Organizers say this years event also recognizes Americas 250th anniversary, bringing an added sense of celebration to the annual holiday tradition in Palm Beach County.

The free community event includes a pool party, lawn games, live music, a barbecue buffet and a fireworks finale scheduled for 9 p.m. The festivities begin with a community pool party from 11 a.m. at the country club pool area. Guests can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games and activities, food and beverages and a poolside satellite bar.

Beginning at 4:30 p.m., families can take part in activities including cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga, face painting and lawn games. Live music from Solstice Reign is expected to begin around 6 p.m. Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, said the golf course will offer one of the best locations to watch the fireworks display. The Clubhouse will also host a Fourth of July barbecue buffet from 4:30 p.m.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds surges ahead in Florida GOP governor's race as Collins sues to remove rival from ballot
cards.body:
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds strengthened his position as the Republican front-runner to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis this week, announcing his campaign and affiliated political committee have raised more than $90 million this cycle, including over $23 million in the second quarter. The campaign recently launched a $20 million statewide advertising buy ahead of Florida's August 18 primary. Donalds picked up endorsements from two statewide officials appointed by DeSantis: Attorney General James Uthmeier and Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia. He also secured backing from the two incoming legislative leaders, Senate President Jim Boyd and House Speaker Sam Garrison. These endorsements carry particular weight in a primary where DeSantis himself has not endorsed a successor, though several figures from his administration have begun supporting Donalds.

While Donalds builds momentum with money and institutional support, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins filed a lawsuit this week to remove Republican candidate James Fishback from the ballot. Collins argues Fishback fails to meet Florida's constitutional requirement that a governor reside in the state for at least seven years before election. The legal complaint highlights Fishback's ties to Washington, D.C., including allegations that he claimed a D.C. property as his primary residence and voted there in 2020. Collins said the challenge was necessary because "election integrity matters."

Fishback denied the allegations, asserting he was born and raised in Florida and accusing Collins of attempting to damage his campaign. Without providing evidence, Fishback suggested Collins was working with Donalds and said his team's first motion would demand both Donalds and Collins release all communications between their campaigns. The legal battle adds uncertainty to the GOP primary as mail ballots prepare to go out and the primary date approaches.

In other Florida political developments this week, state officials moved forward with restrictions targeting undocumented students. The State Board of Education voted to advance rules barring undocumented students from the state's 28 colleges and adult education programs, including GED courses. This follows a separate action by the Board of Governors, which proposed barring undocumented students from Florida's more competitive public universities starting in the 2027-28 academic year, though currently enrolled students would not be affected. Additionally, Gov. DeSantis moved to use a new state law allowing Florida to designate organizations as terrorist groups. The state said it would seek to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood, and Antifa. CAIR and civil rights groups quickly sued in federal court, calling the move unconstitutional and arguing it could threaten the organization's ability to operate in Florida.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board fights judge's order to reinstate teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk Facebook post
cards.teaser: The Martin County School Board filed a court challenge Thursday against an administrative law judge's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a social studie.
cards.body:
The Martin County School Board filed a court challenge Thursday against an administrative law judge's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy suspended over Facebook comments about conservative activist Charlie Kirk. In the filing, the board's attorney argued that Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone's recommendation was not based on competent substantial evidence and that Theobald's post about Kirk was a serious offense warranting his removal.

Theobald, who has taught at Spectrum Academy since 2009, admitted writing the comments calling Kirk racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi but told investigators he posted them on his mother's private Facebook page within a discussion among personal acquaintances and did not intend them for public view. Judge Livingstone cited a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that said disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds, on personal equipment, with no student involvement, violated First Amendment rights. The judge recommended Theobald receive back pay and benefits along with reinstatement. The Martin County School Board retains final authority to decide whether Theobald gets his job back, with no date set for the decision.

cards.headline: Florida advances rules to bar undocumented students from state colleges and adult education programs
cards.teaser: The State Board of Education voted to move forward with rules that would bar undocumented students from Florida's 28 state colleges and adult education programs, including GED preparation courses.
cards.body:
The State Board of Education voted to move forward with rules that would bar undocumented students from Florida's 28 state colleges and adult education programs, including GED preparation courses that can serve as a bridge to college or workforce training. This action follows a separate move by the state university system's Board of Governors, which advanced a plan to bar undocumented students from enrolling at Florida's public universities beginning with the 2027-28 academic year. Currently enrolled students would not be affected under that university proposal.

Supporters of the restrictions argue taxpayer-backed institutions should be reserved for students who are lawfully present in the United States. Immigrant advocates and students opposed the rules, saying they would close doors for young people who grew up in Florida and graduated from Florida schools. Alexander Vallejos, a student Dreamer, said, "We're just asking for an opportunity to earn our future through education. Because when Dreamers succeed, Florida succeeds." These moves come after Florida previously eliminated in-state tuition rates for many undocumented students, including some protected under DACA.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis moves to designate CAIR, Muslim Brotherhood and Antifa as terrorist organizations under new state law
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis said Florida will seek to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood and Antifa as terrorist organizations under a new state law that took effect July 1.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis moved this week to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood and Antifa as terrorist organizations under a new state law that took effect July 1. The law allows the governor and Florida Cabinet to designate organizations based on recommendations from state domestic security officials. DeSantis said Florida will also seek to designate more than 90 federally designated foreign terrorist organizations, including cartel-linked groups and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. If approved by the Cabinet, the designations could block taxpayer funding, contracts or other public support for listed groups. The law also creates penalties for providing material support and could subject some organizations to dissolution under state statute.

CAIR and civil-rights groups quickly sued in federal court, calling the move unconstitutional and warning it could threaten the organization's ability to operate in Florida. Scott McCoy, deputy legal director for the Southern Poverty Law Center, stated that Gov. DeSantis does not have the power to unilaterally brand an organization with this vilifying designation and punish those who support it without due process or judicial review. The lawsuit argues the designation process violates free-speech and due-process rights, while DeSantis and supporters of the law argue the state is acting to combat extremism and protect public institutions.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound man loses fiancee in deadly home fire, community launches fundraiser
cards.teaser: Misty Dawn White, 46, died Monday after a fire broke out inside her Hobe Sound home.
cards.body:
Misty Dawn White, 46, died Monday after a fire broke out inside her Hobe Sound home. The Martin County Sheriff's Office said preliminary findings point to an electrical issue as a possible cause. The fire remains under investigation. White's fiancé, Mark, called his friend Nina Fenn to inform her of White's death. Fenn, who had known White for eight years, returned to the scene in the days following the tragedy. "It's just a terrible shame and awful loss of life," Fenn said.

Friends have launched a fundraiser to help Mark rebuild after the flames destroyed many of his and White's belongings. Fenn described the home as "completely a state of devastation." Fenn remembered White as a Christian woman who loved gardening, plants, and playing piano. "She was always the first to lend a hand. She loves kids; she loves her kids. She loves people," Fenn said. The loss is compounded by previous tragedy Mark has endured. "Mark lost his one and only child, Jacob, and lost him tragically," Fenn said. White's birthday was July 4, meaning she died just days before turning 47. Fenn said White's memory will live on in the hearts of those who loved her.

hero.headline: Juno Beach faces thousands in costs as residents demand fence replacement at JB-7 beach access
hero.teaser: Residents at the Colony Condos say beachgoers have been cutting through their private property since the town removed a fence at the JB-7 public walkway in 2023. The Juno Beach Town Council will take up the fence question during budget discussions July 15.
hero.body:
A missing fence at a public beach access point in Juno Beach has sparked a dispute between condo residents and summer visitors, with replacement costs potentially reaching six figures. Residents at the Colony Condos say people using the JB-7 public walkway have been crossing through their private property since the town removed the old fence in 2023 for safety reasons. With only bushes now marking the boundary between the public path and private land, the problem has escalated during peak summer months.

Lori Hill, a Colony resident, described how the situation has worsened over time. "Lots of cars that just come at random, and then they just park on the spots there," Hill said. "Bushes are pushed back that they cut through those with their coolers and their fishing rods and lawn chairs and everything, and then they just park there all day." She explained that when the fence was in place, the property line was clearly visible to beachgoers. Since its removal, residents have faced repeated confrontations with trespassers. Hill noted that residents previously tried talking to people who crossed onto their property, but many became hostile in response. Now, residents call police to handle the situation instead.

However, not everyone views the problem with the same urgency. Michael House, a beachgoer who walks to JB-7 from a public parking lot several blocks away, said he has never witnessed the issues residents describe. "There's plenty of free parking. If they're damaging property and you know littering and stuff like that might be a different issue," House said. "I have never noticed anyone hopping the fence or the shrubs or anything like that."

The matter was brought before the Juno Beach Town Council recently, where officials stated the town is not obligated to install a fence. Vice Mayor Pro Tem DD Halpern suggested exploring lower-cost alternatives. "I understand fencing is expensive, but I'd like to see maybe we can help them with a lower-cost fence or some combination of split rail and shrubs," Halpern said. Hill expressed hope that the town would act to restore the fence so residents could reclaim their landscaping and private parking areas. The council decided to address the fence question during its upcoming budget discussions scheduled for July 15.

cards.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to win 2026 All-America City Award
cards.teaser: Riviera Beach was selected as one of just 10 communities in the United States to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League. The city earned recognition for bringing residents, government, businesses and organizations together to solve local challenges.
cards.body:
The City of Riviera Beach was named one of just 10 communities in the United States to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, making it the only Florida city selected for the honor this year. The award recognizes communities that bring residents, local government, businesses and organizations together to solve local challenges and create lasting change. Riviera Beach leaders presented the city's efforts to strengthen community engagement at the National Civic League conference in Denver, where the award was announced. Mayor Douglas Lawson called the recognition a proud moment for the city, saying "Little old Riviera Beach is one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars." He noted the city earned the award through a long-term effort to revitalize Riviera Beach and improve quality of life for residents.

City leaders said the recognition reflects years of work focused on improving civic health, strengthening trust between residents and local government, and creating opportunities for the community to play a direct role in shaping the city's future. The city's application highlighted the Riviera Beach Youth Council, which helps high school students become involved in civic leadership, the Citizens Leadership Academy with a 98 percent completion rate, and the Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program providing mini-grants to help longtime homeowners make critical repairs. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited residents for the honor, saying the award brings back community pride. The All-America City Award has been presented annually since 1949.

cards.headline: S.D. Spady Elementary in Delray Beach jumps from C to A rating in state school grades
cards.teaser: S.D. Spady Elementary School made a dramatic leap from a C rating last year to an A this year as the School District of Palm Beach County earned its third consecutive A rating from the state. Principal Rona Tata has led the school for 15 years.
cards.body:
S.D. Spady Elementary School in Delray Beach jumped from a C rating last year to an A this year, one of the biggest success stories as the School District of Palm Beach County earned its third consecutive A rating from the state. Principal Rona Tata, who has spent the last 15 years as principal after serving five years as assistant principal, led the turnaround effort. Community member Chris Ceasar, who attended Spady as a child and now has family members enrolled there, said the jump to an A rating is a huge accomplishment for the community. Tata said staff began taking a closer look at the foundation of student learning three years ago by modifying the school's early childhood curriculum program, which starts at age 3 and combines with kindergarten. Many of those students are now in third grade and performing at higher levels, which contributed to the renewed A rating.

Spady Elementary was one of four district schools to improve from a C rating to an A this year. The others include Dwight D. Eisenhower K-8, Glade View Elementary and West Gate Elementary. The school also fine-tuned its entire academic approach, focusing not only on testing grades but also on challenging students and staff to raise expectations across campus. The school's theme last year was "Be the reason you succeed." Districtwide, 143 district-operated schools, or 84 percent, were rated A or B, up from 120 schools the previous year. The district also achieved a record 93.5 percent graduation rate.

cards.headline: Boca Raton Community High School band to march at National Independence Day Parade in Washington
cards.teaser: The Boca Raton Community High School band has earned a coveted spot in Washington D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade on July 4 and will represent the entire state of Florida. Only bands nominated by state officials get invited to the prestigious event.
cards.body:
The Boca Raton Community High School band has earned an invitation to march in Washington, D.C.'s National Independence Day Parade on July 4 at 10:30 a.m. The band will represent the entire state of Florida at the prestigious event, which only invites bands nominated by state officials. Students will march a full mile along the National Mall, from Constitution Avenue to Independence Avenue.

Junior Lola Cabezas said millions, if not billions, of people will be watching the parade. "It's a lot of pressure, but I think we'll be able to rise to the occasion," she said. Cabezas explained the physical demands of marching band, noting that students must play, breathe and walk while maintaining consistent sound without hearing the steps in the music. Senior Stephin Restivo said the team is focused on marching and timing, adding that everyone will see what the Boca High band is capable of. Band Director Jenn Girdlestone said she has full confidence in her students to represent the country well. Senior Lily Schaffer called it an amazing opportunity that shows how much the program has grown. The parade will be streamed live on YouTube.

cards.headline: Martin County Maritime Response Unit deploys two boats with medics for Fourth of July weekend
cards.teaser: Martin County Maritime Response Unit is deploying two boats with medics on standby in the north and south of the county as hundreds of boaters hit the waterways for Fourth of July weekend. Lt. Brett Harry urges boaters to keep eyes on the water and pack life vests.
cards.body:
Hundreds of boaters are hitting Florida waterways this Fourth of July weekend, prompting Martin County Maritime Response Unit to deploy additional resources. Lt. Brett Harry said his team is expecting significant boat traffic and will have two boats with medics stationed in the north and south of Martin County. "We're just out there to mitigate anybody that needs help, whether it's something as simple as a stubbed toe to anything cardiac related, or potential spinal injuries, or anything like that," Harry said.

Boaters like Brendan and Ashley Shannon, who launched Friday at Sandsprit Park in Martin County with their young daughter and puppy, said safety is their top priority on the water. Harry urged boaters to keep their eyes on the water, designate a driver, and pack life vests, whistles and flotation devices. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said.

cards.headline: Stuart downtown dock closes Sunday for $3 million renovation doubling slip capacity
cards.teaser: Stuart's downtown public dock will close July 6 for renovations projected to be complete by next Fourth of July. The project will expand the dock from 18 to 44 slips for both motorized and non-motorized vessels.
cards.body:
Stuart's downtown public dock will close July 6 for renovations projected to be complete by next Fourth of July. The $3 million project will nearly double the dock's capacity, expanding from 18 to 44 slips for both motorized and non-motorized vessels. The renovation will include a 7,500 square foot fixed dock, a 1,400 square foot floating dock and a smaller floating platform. The project is funded by a state grant and transportation impact fees.

With more than 1,400 boaters using the dock annually, Stuart Mayor Sean Reed said the upgrades address more than capacity. "They're doing it to prevent storm damage during hurricanes and major storms," Reed said. "So the year of waiting will be worth it." During the closure, the city is accommodating businesses and boaters who rely on the dock for drop-off and pick-up. Tiki Taxi & Cruises, which operates off the dock, will be allowed to build a gate at the end of the downtown Stuart dock's non-floating section to board people. Austin Kuyrkendall, director of operations for Tiki Taxi & Cruises, said the solution allows the business to continue operating during construction.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie moves forward on Midway Road expansion and Florida Turnpike interchange
cards.teaser: Last month, the Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance to give 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation to assist with a partial interchange on the Turnpike.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie is moving forward on a major infrastructure project that includes expanding Midway Road and adding a partial interchange to the Florida Turnpike. Last month, the Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance to donate 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation to assist with the interchange. Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, said there is a significant gap between the current entrances and exits to the Turnpike in the city. The interchange is designed to improve accessibility and accommodate growth in the area over the next 20 to 50 years.

FDOT is constructing the $95 million Midway Road Widening Project to address congestion and safety concerns. Crews are currently working on the first phase, widening the road from two lanes to four lanes between Selvitz Road and Jenkins Road. The second widening phase, from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road, remains in the design phase with construction anticipated to begin in Summer 2027. The partial Turnpike interchange is also still in the design phase. The project will include bike and pedestrian paths along with sidewalks. The city council will vote on final approval of the land donation at an upcoming meeting.

cards.headline: California company proposes elevated self-driving transit connecting West Palm Beach to airport
cards.teaser: Glydways will present a proposal to Palm Beach County commissioners Tuesday for an elevated network of autonomous vehicles connecting PBIA to the convention center and nearby Brightline and Tri-Rail stations.
cards.body:
A California-based autonomous transit company is proposing an elevated network of self-driving vehicles connecting downtown West Palm Beach to President Donald J. Trump International Airport. Glydways, which has projects underway in Atlanta and California, will present the proposal to Palm Beach County commissioners Tuesday for initial consideration. The company describes the system as a modern alternative to traditional transit such as light rail, streetcars and people movers.

Small autonomous electric vehicles carrying four to six passengers would travel along a dedicated elevated guideway built above existing roads. The system would bypass traffic congestion entirely, potentially cutting the trip between downtown and the airport to less than 10 minutes. Glydways estimates travel times of seven minutes or less between the convention center and airport and roughly one to two minutes between Tri-Rail and the convention center. While Glydways has not disclosed a specific price tag, Senior Vice President Brian Gettinger said the system would cost a small fraction of a traditional light rail system while offering comparable passenger capacity. He referenced previous South Florida light rail discussions that carried estimates of 400 million to 500 million dollars per mile. Funding could potentially come from Palm Beach County, the City of West Palm Beach, the Florida Department of Transportation, federal transit grants and public-private partnerships. Tuesday's meeting is not expected to approve construction, but rather determine whether the county should formally evaluate the proposal.

Mayor Douglas Lawson expressed pride in the recognition, stating "Little old Riviera Beach is one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars." He credited the award to years of dedicated work aimed at revitalizing the city and improving residents' quality of life. "They're seeing the changes; they're seeing the revitalization and the reimagining of Riviera Beach that we set out so many years to do," Lawson said. City leaders emphasize that the award reflects their commitment to strengthening civic health, building trust between residents and government, and ensuring community members have a direct voice in shaping the city's future.

The city's application highlighted several programs designed to increase civic participation. The Riviera Beach Youth Council engages high school students in civic leadership and advocacy, while the Citizens Leadership Academy provides civic education with a 98 percent completion rate. The Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program offers mini-grants to help longtime homeowners make necessary repairs to their properties. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited residents for making the achievement possible. "This award is a tribute to the heart and determination of our residents," Miller-Anderson said. "Every event we host, every project we complete, and every challenge we overcome happens because our community shows up for one another."

The All-America City Award, presented annually since 1949, ranks among the nation's most respected civic honors. City officials say the designation sends a powerful message that Riviera Beach is a community where collaboration produces results and residents actively shape the city's direction. The award also positions Riviera Beach for future opportunities and continued growth. Other cities receiving the 2026 award include Chelsea, Massachusetts; Franklin, Tennessee; Harlingen, Texas; Montgomery, Alabama; Morrisville, North Carolina; Norfolk, Virginia; North Charleston, South Carolina; Roanoke, Virginia; and Woodburn, Oregon.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie moves forward on Midway Road expansion and Florida Turnpike interchange
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance last month to give 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation to support a partial interchange at Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County. According to Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, there is a significant gap between the entrances and exits to the Turnpike currently in Port St. Lucie. Samples said the interchange is designed to accommodate growth that has already occurred and growth expected over the next 20 to 50 years.

FDOT is constructing the $95 million Midway Road Widening Project to address congestion and safety. Crews are currently working on the first phase, widening the road from two lanes to four lanes from Selvitz Road to Jenkins Road. The second phase from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road is still in the design phase, with construction anticipated to begin in Summer 2027. The project will also add bike and pedestrian paths along with sidewalks. The partial interchange for the Turnpike remains in the design phase. City council will vote on final approval to give the land at an upcoming meeting.

cards.headline: Martin County maritime teams prepare for hundreds of Fourth of July boaters
cards.teaser: Martin County Maritime Response Unit will have two boats with medics on standby in north and south Martin County as hundreds of boaters are expected on the water for the Fourth of July weekend.
cards.body:
Hundreds of boaters are expected to hit Florida's waterways this Fourth of July weekend, prompting local maritime safety crews to prepare for potential emergencies. Lt. Brett Harry with Martin County Maritime Response Unit said his team will position two boats with medics on standby in Martin County's north and south areas to assist boaters throughout the holiday. "We're just out there to mitigate anybody that needs help, whether it's something as simple as a stubbed toe to anything cardiac related, or potential spinal injuries, or anything like that," Harry said.

Boaters launched Friday from Sandsprit Park in Martin County with safety as a priority. Among them were Brendan and Ashley Shannon, who took their young daughter and puppy out on the water. Harry emphasized that boaters should keep their eyes on the water, designate a driver, and pack life vests, whistles and flotation devices before setting sail. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound community raises funds for man who lost fiance in deadly home fire
cards.teaser: Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside the couple's home in Hobe Sound. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause.
cards.body:
A Hobe Sound man is leaning on his community after losing his fiancée in a deadly home fire. Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside the couple's home. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause. The fire remains under investigation. Nina Fenn, a friend of White's for eight years, learned of the death through a phone call from White's fiancé, Mark. Friends have since launched a fundraiser to help Mark rebuild after the flames destroyed many of his and White's belongings. Fenn described the home as "completely a state of devastation."

Fenn reflected on her friendship with White, describing her as a Christian woman who loved gardening, plants and playing the piano. "She was always the first to lend a hand," Fenn said. "She loves kids; she loves her kids. She loves people." The loss is compounded by grief Mark has already endured. "Mark lost his one and only child, Jacob, and lost him tragically," Fenn said. The timing of White's death adds another layer of heartbreak, as Misty's birthday is the Fourth of July. She passed just a few days before her birthday.

cards.headline: Fourth of July cookout costs rise 4 percent as ground beef and buns see largest increases
cards.teaser: According to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey, a holiday meal for 10 now costs $73.82, up 4 percent from a year ago.
cards.body:
The Fourth of July cookout tradition is getting more expensive this year. According to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey, a holiday meal for 10 now costs $73.82, up 4 percent from a year ago. Inflation is driving the increases across multiple items. Ground beef prices have risen 5.5 percent, while buns are up 7.7 percent. Strawberries, impacted by a Florida frost, have seen the largest increase at 12.4 percent. Ice cream prices are also up 5.3 percent.

Not all cookout staples are more expensive this year. Potato prices have decreased, offering savings for those planning potato chips or salads. Corn prices have fluctuated, though locally grown corn from the Glades can provide the best deals. Budgeting expert Andrea Woroch recommends families shop more strategically by comparing prices across stores to find the best deals on their grocery lists. She emphasized that cutting down on food waste through meal planning is the biggest opportunity for families to manage costs during the holiday season.

cards.headline: Breast cancer patient denied insurance coverage for reconstruction hours before surgery
cards.teaser: Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma three months ago. Less than 24 hours before her reconstruction surgery, her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for the procedure.
cards.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma three months ago and decided to undergo a double bilateral mastectomy with reconstruction. Less than 24 hours before her reconstruction surgery, her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for the procedure. According to her denial letter, the surgery involved a surgical mesh called GalaFlex, which the insurer considers "investigational" with "no or not enough proof it improves health." GalaFlex is a synthetic surgical mesh popular among plastic surgeons and FDA-approved for some uses in the body, but it is not approved for breast reconstruction and remains an off-label, investigational treatment. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated that the treatment's "efficacy and safety for breast cancer patients have not been determined."

Dr. Alicia Billington, Clark's plastic surgeon, uses GalaFlex mesh on most of her breast reconstruction patients and believes insurance companies should reconsider their coverage policies. Billington has been a vocal critic of insurance denials, sharing Clark's case on social media and calling for policy changes. Last year, after investigative reporting shared breast cancer patients' stories, Cigna became the first and only major insurer to start approving GalaFlex for breast reconstruction. Anthem responded by stating the mesh "does not currently meet the standards required for coverage by our medical policy." Despite the denial, Clark received her reconstruction surgery with GalaFlex mesh more than a week ago, and she and Billington continue fighting the denial.

cards.headline: Autonomous transit company proposes elevated network connecting West Palm Beach to airport
cards.teaser: Glydways, a California-based autonomous transit company, is proposing an elevated network of self-driving vehicles that would connect downtown West Palm Beach to President Donald J. Trump International Airport.
cards.body:
Glydways, a California-based autonomous transit company with projects underway in Atlanta and California, will present its proposal to Palm Beach County commissioners Tuesday for initial consideration. The elevated network would connect downtown West Palm Beach to President Donald J. Trump International Airport, the convention center, and nearby Brightline and Tri-Rail stations. Small autonomous electric vehicles carrying four to six passengers would travel along a dedicated elevated guideway built above existing roads, bypassing traffic congestion. The company estimates travel times of seven minutes or less between the convention center and airport and one to two minutes between Tri-Rail and the convention center, potentially cutting the downtown-to-airport trip to less than 10 minutes.

Senior Vice President Brian Gettinger described the system as a "horizontal elevator" that functions as a modern alternative to light rail, streetcars and people movers. While Glydways has not disclosed a specific price tag, Gettinger said the system would cost "a small fraction" of traditional light rail, which previous South Florida discussions estimated at $400 million to $500 million per mile. Potential funding sources include Palm Beach County, the City of West Palm Beach, the Florida Department of Transportation, federal transit grants and public-private partnerships. Gettinger said the service would be priced at transit levels rather than private rideshare rates and would require local employees for operations centers and maintenance facilities.

hero.headline: Saint Andrew's Scots football targets state title after 10-2 season and district championship
hero.body:
The Saint Andrew's Scots football program is focused on a state title run this fall after completing last season with a 10-2 record and a district championship. The team's second-round playoff exit has motivated players and coaches to pursue a deeper postseason run in 2026. The Scots are putting in significant work during summer workouts to prepare for what they believe could be their best season yet.

Head coach Jimmy Robertson emphasized the experience and continuity of his senior class. "Most of these seniors are four-year seniors. I mean, if not the majority of them came from the middle school as well. So they know how things are run. They had a lot of success in their career, and hopefully their senior year is the best season that we've had," Robertson said. This veteran leadership has been instrumental in the program's recent success and is expected to guide the team's next chapter.

To challenge themselves and prepare for increased playoff competition, the Scots deliberately scheduled tougher opponents for the upcoming season. Senior Jack Williams explained the reasoning behind this approach. "We knew that we wanted to take our program to the next level. So we really have a challenging schedule for this year because we wanna compete. That's what we wanna do and we wanna take that next level, and it's by playing against really good teams that we do that and attract new people," Williams said. The team recognizes that improving their playoff performance requires facing quality competition throughout the regular season.

The definition of success for Saint Andrew's this season extends beyond regular season wins. Senior Jack Whelche highlighted what truly matters to the program. "A better year is just gonna be going farther in the playoffs. Obviously we wanna go undefeated in the season, but that doesn't matter if we keep losing in the second round of the playoffs. We just gotta go farther than that, that's all that matters," Whelche said. Senior Edmyer St. Jean emphasized how the summer training program builds momentum heading into fall. "It just adds up every day as something like to look forward to. Work harder so we can see the results when we come off the season positive and break our record," St. Jean said. With their veteran leadership, challenging schedule, and focused approach to summer preparation, the Scots appear positioned to make a legitimate push toward the state championship.

cards.headline: Martin County maritime teams deploy two boats with medics for Fourth of July weekend
cards.teaser: Martin County Maritime Response Unit will have two boats with medics on standby in north and south county as hundreds of boaters celebrate the holiday weekend.
cards.body:
Hundreds of boaters are expected on Florida waterways this Fourth of July weekend. The Martin County Maritime Response Unit will deploy two boats with medics stationed in north and south Martin County to respond to emergencies. Lt. Brett Harry said the team is prepared to help boaters with any medical need, ranging from minor injuries to serious conditions. "We're just out there to mitigate anybody that needs help, whether it's something as simple as a stubbed toe to anything cardiac related, or potential spinal injuries, or anything like that," Harry said.

Boaters Brendan and Ashley Shannon launched from Sandsprit Park in Martin County on Friday with their young daughter and puppy. Harry urged all boaters to prioritize safety by keeping their eyes on the water, designating a sober driver, and packing life vests, whistles and flotation devices. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound woman dies in home fire days before her birthday
cards.teaser: Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out in her Hobe Sound home. Her fiance Mark and friends are raising money to help him rebuild.
cards.body:
Misty Dawn White, 46, died Monday in a home fire in Hobe Sound. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause. The fire remains under investigation. Friends have launched a fundraiser to help White's fiancé Mark rebuild after the flames destroyed many of his and White's belongings.

Nina Fenn, a friend of White's for eight years, learned of the death through a phone call from Mark. "We received a call from Mark stating that Misty had passed away in a fire," Fenn said. Fenn described White as a Christian woman who loved gardening, plants and playing piano. "She loves kids; she loves her kids. She loves people," Fenn said. White's birthday was July 4, meaning she died just days before her birthday. Fenn noted that Mark previously lost his only child, Jacob, in a tragedy.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board fights judge's order to reinstate teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk comments
cards.teaser: The Martin County School Board filed a court motion Thursday challenging a judge's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a Spectrum Academy teacher suspended for Facebook comments about Charlie Kirk.
cards.body:
The Martin County School Board filed a court motion Thursday opposing Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy since 2009. Theobald was suspended last year after Facebook comments labeling Charlie Kirk as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi. The board's attorney argued the Facebook post about Kirk was a "serious offense" and that removing Theobald was appropriate. In the filing, the board claimed "numerous findings ... are not based upon competent substantial evidence" in Livingstone's order.

In her order issued last month, Livingstone cited a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that found disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds on personal equipment with no student involvement violated First Amendment rights. She recommended Theobald receive back pay and benefits. According to an investigation report, Theobald admitted writing the comments but said they were posted on his mother's private Facebook page "within a discussion among personal acquaintances" and were not intended for public view. The school board retains final authority on whether Theobald gets his job back. No timeline for a final decision has been announced.

cards.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to win 2026 All-America City Award
cards.teaser: Riviera Beach is one of just 10 communities nationwide to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, and the only Florida city selected this year.
cards.body:
Riviera Beach has been named one of 10 communities nationwide to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, making it the only Florida city selected for the honor this year. The award was announced during the National Civic League conference in Denver and recognizes communities that bring residents, local government, businesses and organizations together to solve local challenges and create lasting change. Mayor Douglas Lawson said the recognition reflects the city's long-term effort to revitalize Riviera Beach and improve quality of life for residents. "Little old Riviera Beach is one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars," Lawson said. "They're seeing the changes; they're seeing the revitalization and the reimagining of Riviera Beach that we set out so many years to do."

Riviera Beach's application highlighted three civic programs: the Riviera Beach Youth Council, which involves high school students in civic leadership and advocacy; the Citizens Leadership Academy, a civic education initiative with a 98 percent completion rate; and the Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program, which provides mini-grants to longtime homeowners for critical repairs. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited residents for the honor. "This award is a tribute to the heart and determination of our residents," Miller-Anderson said. She noted that winning the award reinforces the city's positive momentum and brings back community pride.

cards.headline: Breast cancer patient's insurance denies reconstruction surgery hours before procedure
cards.teaser: Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield denied coverage for Beth Clark's breast reconstruction surgery less than 24 hours before the scheduled procedure, citing GalaFlex mesh as investigational.
cards.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma three months ago and underwent a full double bilateral mastectomy. Less than 24 hours before her scheduled reconstruction surgery, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield denied coverage for the procedure, which involved GalaFlex surgical mesh. The denial letter stated the treatment is "investigational" and "there is no or not enough proof it improves health." GalaFlex is a synthetic surgical mesh approved by the FDA for some uses in the body but not for breast reconstruction, making it an off-label, investigational and experimental treatment. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated its "efficacy and safety for breast cancer patients have not been determined."

Dr. Alicia Billington, Clark's plastic surgeon, uses GalaFlex mesh on most of her breast reconstruction patients and argues it produces fewer complications than other options. "This product is giving my patients the least amount of complications, and other plastic surgeons as well," Billington said. Despite Anthem's denial, Clark received the reconstruction surgery with GalaFlex mesh a little more than a week ago after Billington found a mechanism to make it happen. Last year, Cigna became the first and only major insurer to start approving GalaFlex for breast reconstruction, following investigative reporting by Katie LaGrone and photojournalist Matthew Apthorp as part of their "Patient No More" series.

cards.headline: Lantana veteran gets roof completed and lien removed after WPTV steps in
cards.teaser: Stephen McCoy, a disabled and retired veteran in Lantana, had a nearly $7,000 lien removed from his home after WPTV contacted the roofing contractor.
cards.body:
Stephen McCoy, a disabled and retired veteran in Lantana, turned to WPTV for help after months of frustration with Seabreeze Roofing and Sheet Metal in Boynton Beach. McCoy hired the company to replace his nearly 20-year-old roof ahead of hurricane season and made six payments totaling more than $17,000. After the work was mostly complete, McCoy said the contractor left two holes unfinished on the back of his home and stopped responding to his calls, texts and emails. Between January 10 and February 5, McCoy made numerous attempts to contact the company, including visiting the building in person two or three times.

The situation worsened when Gulfeagle Supply filed a nearly $7,000 lien against McCoy's property, claiming it had furnished materials to Seabreeze Roofing but was not paid. When WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey spoke with the owner of Seabreeze Roofing about the unpaid materials and lien, he declined to comment on camera citing legal reasons. Within an hour of that conversation, Hussey returned to McCoy's home with a final waiver of lien signed by Gulfeagle Supply and notarized, lifting the lien from his property. The contractor also sent workers back to fix the two problem areas on McCoy's roof.

hero.headline: North Palm Beach hosts Fourth of July fireworks and pool party at country club
hero.teaser: North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse will host a full day of free community activities on July 4, including a pool party, live music, lawn games and fireworks at 9 p.m.
hero.body:
North Palm Beach residents and visitors will celebrate Independence Day with a full day of family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4. Organizers say this years event also recognizes Americas 250th anniversary, bringing an added sense of celebration to the annual holiday tradition in Palm Beach County.

The free community event includes a pool party, lawn games, live music, a barbecue buffet and a fireworks finale scheduled for 9 p.m. The festivities begin with a community pool party from 11 a.m. at the country club pool area. Guests can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games and activities, food and beverages and a poolside satellite bar.

Beginning at 4:30 p.m., families can take part in activities including cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga, face painting and lawn games. Live music from Solstice Reign is expected to begin around 6 p.m. Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, said the golf course will offer one of the best locations to watch the fireworks display. The Clubhouse will also host a Fourth of July barbecue buffet from 4:30 p.m.

cards.headline: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach offers sea turtle programs through September
cards.body:
Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season through September. The center provides seasonal experiences including guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program, Hatchling Releases, Tidal Tots and Plastic Free July Community Action Day. According to the center, these programs are designed to give visitors an opportunity to learn more about sea turtle conservation along one of the world's busiest sea turtle nesting beaches.

The Turtle Walk program allows participants to observe the nesting process while learning about sea turtle biology, conservation and ongoing research efforts. Educational demonstrations may include the use of red-light headlamps, amber lighting, night scopes and research tag scanning equipment. Loggerhead Marinelife Center's education and research departments work together during nesting season to collect and analyze data related to nesting activity and hatchling success. Sea turtle nesting season in Florida typically runs from March through October. Registration information and program details are available through Loggerhead Marinelife Center.

hero.headline: Byron Donalds surges ahead in Florida GOP governor's race as Collins sues to remove rival from ballot
hero.body:
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds strengthened his position as the Republican front-runner to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis this week, announcing his campaign and affiliated political committee have raised more than $90 million this cycle, including over $23 million in the second quarter. The campaign recently launched a $20 million statewide advertising buy ahead of Florida's August 18 primary. Donalds picked up endorsements from two statewide officials appointed by DeSantis: Attorney General James Uthmeier and Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia. He also secured backing from the two incoming legislative leaders, Senate President Jim Boyd and House Speaker Sam Garrison. These endorsements carry particular weight in a primary where DeSantis himself has not endorsed a successor, though several figures from his administration have begun supporting Donalds.

While Donalds builds momentum with money and institutional support, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins filed a lawsuit this week to remove Republican candidate James Fishback from the ballot. Collins argues Fishback fails to meet Florida's constitutional requirement that a governor reside in the state for at least seven years before election. The legal complaint highlights Fishback's ties to Washington, D.C., including allegations that he claimed a D.C. property as his primary residence and voted there in 2020. Collins said the challenge was necessary because "election integrity matters."

Fishback denied the allegations, asserting he was born and raised in Florida and accusing Collins of attempting to damage his campaign. Without providing evidence, Fishback suggested Collins was working with Donalds and said his team's first motion would demand both Donalds and Collins release all communications between their campaigns. The legal battle adds uncertainty to the GOP primary as mail ballots prepare to go out and the primary date approaches.

In other Florida political developments this week, state officials moved forward with restrictions targeting undocumented students. The State Board of Education voted to advance rules barring undocumented students from the state's 28 colleges and adult education programs, including GED courses. This follows a separate action by the Board of Governors, which proposed barring undocumented students from Florida's more competitive public universities starting in the 2027-28 academic year, though currently enrolled students would not be affected. Additionally, Gov. DeSantis moved to use a new state law allowing Florida to designate organizations as terrorist groups. The state said it would seek to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood, and Antifa. CAIR and civil rights groups quickly sued in federal court, calling the move unconstitutional and arguing it could threaten the organization's ability to operate in Florida.

cards.headline: DeSantis allies accuse Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' wife of running anonymous accounts attacking governor
cards.teaser: Multiple social media accounts were deactivated after allegations they were tied to Layla Collins, wife of Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, who is running for governor.
cards.body:
Multiple X accounts were suddenly deactivated after allegations they were tied to Layla Collins, wife of Lt. Gov. Jay Collins. The accusations came from prominent veterans of Gov. Ron DeSantis' communications team, including Christina Pushaw, a communications specialist in the Governor's Office, and Jeremy Redfern, Deputy Chief of Staff to Attorney General James Uthmeier. Pushaw shared information posted by Promota CEO Robert Salvador that showed the account @FSUdude01670 appeared connected to a phone number similar to a known number and email used by Layla Collins. Florida Politics obtained screenshots verifying this through two-factor authentication. Pushaw also identified a second account, @bobnamy1, that she said appeared tied to Layla Collins.

Pushaw said the content of @bobnamy1 suggested it existed entirely to advance Jay Collins' political ambitions as he runs for Governor. "Account content is entirely comprised of two types of posts: Promoting Jay Collins, and attacking people who didn't endorse Jay, including the governor," Pushaw posted. Redfern also criticized the accounts publicly, stating "The FSUDude account was tied directly to her personal cell phone number." After both officials leveled their criticisms, the accounts were deactivated. Both Pushaw and Redfern previously served as Press Secretaries for DeSantis. Redfern now works for Uthmeier, who has endorsed U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds for Governor. DeSantis appointed Jay Collins as Lieutenant Governor last year but has declined to endorse a preferred successor in the Governor's race.

cards.headline: Florida advances rules to bar undocumented students from state colleges and adult education programs
cards.teaser: The State Board of Education voted to move forward with rules that would bar undocumented students from Florida's 28 state colleges and adult education programs, including GED preparation courses.
cards.body:
The State Board of Education voted to move forward with rules that would bar undocumented students from Florida's 28 state colleges and adult education programs, including GED preparation courses that can serve as a bridge to college or workforce training. This action follows a separate move by the state university system's Board of Governors, which advanced a plan to bar undocumented students from enrolling at Florida's public universities beginning with the 2027-28 academic year. Currently enrolled students would not be affected under that university proposal.

Supporters of the restrictions argue taxpayer-backed institutions should be reserved for students who are lawfully present in the United States. Immigrant advocates and students opposed the rules, saying they would close doors for young people who grew up in Florida and graduated from Florida schools. Alexander Vallejos, a student Dreamer, said, "We're just asking for an opportunity to earn our future through education. Because when Dreamers succeed, Florida succeeds." These moves come after Florida previously eliminated in-state tuition rates for many undocumented students, including some protected under DACA.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg selects $8.1 billion plan to redevelop Tropicana Field site with housing, museums and parks
cards.teaser: St. Petersburg Mayor Ken Welch selected The Burg Bid proposal as the city's preferred path forward for redeveloping Tropicana Field and the surrounding Historic Gas Plant District.
cards.body:
St. Petersburg selected The Burg Bid, led by Blake Investment Partners and Related Group, as the city's preferred redevelopment plan for the Tropicana Field site. The $8.1 billion proposal would transform stadium parking and public land into a mixed-use district featuring housing, hotels, offices, retail, cultural institutions, workforce training, public art and entertainment space. The team proposes purchasing 58 acres of city-owned land for $275 million, valuing the full land package at $405 million when including $130 million in land the city would retain. A $20 million deposit would accompany execution of a purchase and sale agreement.

The plan centers on Samuel Davis Park, a 13-acre civic and cultural space that would include The Woodson African American Museum of Florida, a planned Museum of Public Art, a Discovery Center, event lawns, a playground, a splash pad, café areas, public art and a concert lawn. The proposal calls for 3,600 income-restricted housing units over a 15-year buildout, with 1,800 units in the Historic Gas Plant District and 1,800 on complementary sites elsewhere in St. Petersburg. The district would be built in three phases of approximately five years each, with early development potentially beginning before Tropicana Field's demolition. The Tampa Bay Rays' lease with the city ends after the 2028 season.

cards.headline: Secretary of State Cord Byrd asks court to keep Paula Stark off ballot after incomplete filing
cards.teaser: Secretary of State Cord Byrd is asking courts to keep Paula Stark off the ballot after the St. Cloud Republican failed to submit required paperwork by the qualifying deadline.
cards.body:
Paula Stark's incomplete qualifying materials were timestamped less than 30 minutes before the noon deadline on June 12, and she is now suing to get on the ballot. In the state's response to her Leon Circuit Court lawsuit, Secretary of State Cord Byrd is asking the courts to keep Stark off the ballot and cast doubt on her claims about an alleged paperwork mix-up. Five state employees gave sworn written court declarations stating that Stark's treasurer and partner, Joel Davis, never submitted the crucial Form 6 to them nor was he accidentally handed it back when he submitted the rest of the paperwork in the final hour of the qualifying window. Byrd argued in his response that had Stark or Davis exercised care by questioning why the Form 6 was allegedly handed back, the mistake would have been discovered while Davis was at the Division.

Three weeks after the qualifying deadline passed, Stark still hasn't submitted Form 6, said Election Records Division Bureau Chief Erica Ikay Reeve. Stark was one of 12 candidates who didn't properly turn in Form 6, a public disclosure of financial interests. Half of them corrected the problems and still qualified. Reeve also noted Stark's years of paperwork problems, including a campaign finance report filed over one month late, audits that found inconsistent amounts transferred between campaign and office accounts, and unpaid fines. The state revoked Stark's Friends of Paula political committee in November over $16,000 in unpaid fines from missed campaign finance deadlines. If Stark is not on the ballot, the August Primary for House District 47 opens to all voters to decide between Democrats Jorge Figueroa and Anthony Nieves.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis moves to designate CAIR, Muslim Brotherhood and Antifa as terrorist organizations under new state law
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis said Florida will seek to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood and Antifa as terrorist organizations under a new state law that took effect July 1.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis moved this week to designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood and Antifa as terrorist organizations under a new state law that took effect July 1. The law allows the governor and Florida Cabinet to designate organizations based on recommendations from state domestic security officials. DeSantis said Florida will also seek to designate more than 90 federally designated foreign terrorist organizations, including cartel-linked groups and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. If approved by the Cabinet, the designations could block taxpayer funding, contracts or other public support for listed groups. The law also creates penalties for providing material support and could subject some organizations to dissolution under state statute.

CAIR and civil-rights groups quickly sued in federal court, calling the move unconstitutional and warning it could threaten the organization's ability to operate in Florida. Scott McCoy, deputy legal director for the Southern Poverty Law Center, stated that Gov. DeSantis does not have the power to unilaterally brand an organization with this vilifying designation and punish those who support it without due process or judicial review. The lawsuit argues the designation process violates free-speech and due-process rights, while DeSantis and supporters of the law argue the state is acting to combat extremism and protect public institutions.

cards.headline: Woodson African American Museum of Florida to reopen July 11 with Smithsonian-linked America 250 exhibition
cards.teaser: The Woodson's newly renovated museum is set to reopen July 11 as part of its 20th anniversary celebration, coinciding with the opening of a Smithsonian-linked America 250 exhibition.
cards.body:
The Woodson African American Museum of Florida will reopen July 11 as part of its 20th anniversary celebration, featuring a Smithsonian-linked "Many Voices One Nation — Our Community" exhibition. The museum was selected as one of only three Florida organizations to present this exhibition.

The Woodson's permanent home is planned within the Burg Bid proposal for redeveloping Tropicana Field and the Historic Gas Plant District. The proposal, selected by St. Petersburg Mayor Ken Welch as the city's preferred path forward, places the museum within Samuel Davis Park along a diagonal pedestrian corridor called the Legacy Link. WJArchitects designed the permanent home, which CEO Thompson Whitney Blake described as "evocative" and "architecturally jaw dropping." The museum would serve as an anchor and civic landmark for the Gas Plant District within 18.5 acres of public park space. The Burg Bid proposal preserves the original gas tank footprint within Samuel Davis Park and weaves historic references throughout the Legacy Link, honoring the predominantly Black Gas Plant neighborhood that was razed decades ago to make way for Tropicana Field.

hero.headline: Martin County Maritime Response Unit deploys two boats with medics for Fourth of July weekend
hero.teaser: Hundreds of boaters hit Martin County waterways Friday to celebrate the Fourth of July weekend. The Martin County Maritime Response Unit will have two boats with medics on standby in the north and south parts of the county.
hero.body:
Hundreds of boaters are expected to take to the water across Florida this Fourth of July weekend, and Martin County is preparing for the surge. Lt. Brett Harry with the Martin County Maritime Response Unit says his team is ready to respond to any emergencies that may arise. The unit will position two boats with medics on standby, with one deployed in north Martin County and another in the south to ensure coverage across the area.

The Martin County School Board filed a court document Thursday arguing against Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy who was suspended last year following social media comments about Charlie Kirk. The board's attorney characterized Theobald's Facebook post about Kirk as a "serious offense" and said removing him from his position was appropriate.

Theobald, who has taught at Spectrum Academy since 2009, described Kirk as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi in comments posted on his mother's private Facebook page within a discussion among personal acquaintances. According to an investigation report, Theobald admitted writing the comments but said they were not intended for public view. Last month, Livingstone issued an order citing a Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds on personal equipment with no student involvement violates First Amendment rights. The judge also recommended Theobald receive back pay and benefits. The school board retains final authority on whether Theobald returns to his teaching position, with no date currently set for a final decision.

cards.headline: Breast cancer patient denied insurance coverage for reconstruction surgery hours before procedure
cards.teaser: Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma three months ago. Less than 24 hours before her reconstruction surgery, her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for the procedure.
cards.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma three months ago and underwent a full double bilateral mastectomy with plans for reconstruction surgery. Less than 24 hours before the procedure, her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for the surgery involving a surgical mesh called GalaFlex. According to the denial letter, the surgery is considered "investigational" and lacks sufficient proof that it improves health. GalaFlex is a synthetic surgical mesh approved by the FDA for some uses in the body but not for breast reconstruction, making it an off-label and experimental treatment. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated that the treatment's "efficacy and safety for breast cancer patients have not been determined."

Despite the denial, Clark received her reconstruction surgery with the GalaFlex mesh a little more than a week ago, thanks to her plastic surgeon Dr. Alicia Billington finding a mechanism to make it happen. Billington uses GalaFlex mesh on most of her breast reconstruction patients and says the product gives patients the least amount of complications. She has been a vocal critic of insurance denials, recently sharing Clark's case and calling for policy changes. In response to Clark's denial, Anthem said the mesh "does not currently meet the standards required for coverage by our medical policy," though the company noted it covers many other evidence-based alternatives. Last year, Cigna became the first and only major insurer to start approving GalaFlex for breast reconstruction.

hero.headline: Fourth of July cookout costs up 4% in Florida as ground beef and strawberries rise

hero.body:
The cost of preparing a Fourth of July cookout for ten people has increased 4 percent compared to last year, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's Summer Cookout Cost Survey. Families can now expect to spend $73.82 for a holiday meal, a reflection of broader inflationary pressures affecting grocery prices across the country and in Florida specifically.

Several key items driving the price increase stand out in the survey data. Ground beef prices have climbed 5.5 percent, while hamburger buns rose 7.7 percent. Florida's recent frost dealt a significant blow to the strawberry crop, pushing prices up 12.4 percent. Ice cream, a popular Fourth of July dessert, increased 5.3 percent. These increases represent the primary cost drivers for traditional cookout menus. However, not all items on holiday shopping lists have become more expensive. Potato prices have actually declined this year, offering some relief for families planning to serve potato salads or baked potatoes. Corn prices have varied throughout the season, but locally grown corn from the Glades can provide the best value for shoppers.

To manage rising grocery costs, budgeting expert Andrea Woroch recommends a strategic approach to shopping. Consumers should compare prices across different stores to identify the best deals for items on their shopping lists. Woroch emphasizes that reducing food waste is crucial for families trying to control expenses, and creating a meal plan serves as an effective first step in this process. "It's really important to shop savvier than ever, it is comparing the stores to see who has the best deals for the groceries on your list, the biggest thing for families is cutting down the food waste, and that begins with a meal plan," Woroch said.

Shoppers interviewed about their holiday plans highlighted the variety of cookout traditions families enjoy. Some plan to prepare hamburgers with coleslaw and chips for lunch, followed by a dinner of burnt ends and mashed potatoes with fresh broccoli. Others described simpler menus featuring hamburgers, beef, steak, and baked potatoes. Despite the inflationary pressures affecting prices this Fourth of July, these traditional cookout favorites remain popular choices for holiday celebrations, even as families adjust their budgets to accommodate higher costs.
